lesson.title: Growth Without Gaps: Continuity of Exponentials and Logarithms
lesson.summary: Exponential functions are continuous across all real numbers, and logarithmic functions, as their inverses, are continuous across their entire domain of positive numbers.
lesson.body:
Exponential functions describe processes like population growth, compound interest, and radioactive decay, and for those models to make physical sense, small changes in time should produce small changes in the quantity being modeled, not sudden jumps. That requirement is exactly continuity, and it holds for every exponential function b^x with base b greater than 0: b^x is continuous at every real number x. Its inverse, the logarithmic function, is continuous too, but only on the domain where it is defined.

For an exponential function f(x) = b^x with b > 0, continuity at every real number follows from the fact that b^x varies smoothly as the exponent varies smoothly, which can be checked using the same translation trick used for sine and cosine: b^(a+h) = b^a times b^h. As h approaches 0, b^h approaches b^0 = 1, so b^(a+h) approaches b^a times 1 = b^a, matching f(a). Since a was arbitrary, b^x is continuous everywhere.

Logarithmic functions are defined as the inverse of exponential functions: log base b of x is the power to which b must be raised to get x, and its domain is restricted to positive numbers, since a positive base raised to any real power is always positive. Continuity of the logarithm then follows from a general principle: a continuous function that is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing on an interval has a continuous inverse on the corresponding interval. Because b^x is continuous and strictly monotonic, its inverse log base b of x is continuous at every point in its domain, the open interval from 0 to infinity.

For a worked example, verify continuity of f(x) = e^x at x = 0. As x approaches 0, e^x approaches e^0 = 1, which matches f(0) = 1 exactly, confirming continuity at that point. The same translation argument used above shows this holds at every real number a, since e^(a+h) = e^a times e^h, and e^h approaches 1 as h approaches 0, so e^(a+h) approaches e^a.

For the logarithmic side, consider g(x) = ln(x) at x = 1. Direct evaluation gives g(1) = ln(1) = 0, and since ln x is continuous on its domain, the limit of ln x as x approaches 1 also equals ln(1) = 0, matching g(1) exactly. It is essential to remember the domain restriction here: ln(x) is simply not defined for x = 0 or for negative x, so there is no meaningful question of continuity at those inputs. Continuity claims about logarithms always carry the implicit qualifier on their domain.

Together with polynomials, rational functions, and trigonometric functions, exponential and logarithmic functions round out the standard toolkit of continuous elementary functions. Sums, products, quotients, and compositions of these building blocks remain continuous wherever they are defined, which is precisely the kind of well-behaved setup the Intermediate Value Theorem, discussed next, depends on.
